planting.note: Scatter seed in fall directly where it will grow, since it resents transplanting once its taproot is established; a light raking-in and the first rains are usually enough to trigger germination.

directions: A fast, self-sowing annual with a strong, pleasant minty-pungent fragrance and dense purple flower heads, this mint draws bees, native bees, and several moth and butterfly species, making it useful as a quick-filling wildflower-meadow component or gap-filler among slower perennials. Choose a dry, open, sunny site with lean soil, mimicking the disturbed woodland and forest-edge openings where it grows wild, and let a portion of the stand go to seed each year to maintain a self-sustaining population. It finishes its life cycle by midsummer, so interplant it with later-emerging perennials.

planting.note: Direct-sow or root softwood cuttings in fall on the east side of a boulder or shrub where morning sun reaches it but afternoon heat is buffered, extending the bloom season.

directions: A gray-green, lemon-scented subshrub with pale pink flower heads, this monardella blooms longer when given relief from the hottest afternoon sun and is a strong draw for butterflies, with fine, needle-like foliage adding textural contrast to a rock garden or dry slope planting. Plant in sharply draining, lean, rocky or gravelly soil, and resist amending with rich soil or heavy mulch against the crown. Light pruning after bloom keeps the slender stems from sprawling and encourages denser regrowth the following year.

planting.note: Divide or sow in fall into lean, fast-draining soil near the coast in full sun, or with afternoon shade further inland; water occasionally in the first dry season, then taper off.

directions: An uncommon, disjunct California endemic with woolly-backed leaves and pink-to-purple flower heads, this monardella provides nectar for native bees and butterflies, and its rarity in cultivation makes it a genuine conservation-minded addition for native-plant gardens in its home range. The decumbent to erect stems benefit from being tucked among rocks or companion shrubs that keep leaves out of standing water during winter rains. Because wild populations are limited and disjunct, source seed or plants of known local provenance.

planting.note: Divide or sow in fall into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil under light shade from oaks or chaparral shrubs; give it room to spread slowly by rhizome.

directions: A rhizomatous subshrub with fuzzy green leaves backed in white wool and inch-wide purple flower heads, this monardella gives strong two-tone foliage interest even between bloom cycles, well suited to chaparral and oak-woodland gardens in southern California where it spreads gently by rhizome rather than aggressive runners. An occasional light shearing in late winter removes old flowering stems and keeps the clump from looking leggy. Established plants need only occasional deep watering through the dry months and should never sit in soggy or heavy clay soil.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated seed or cuttings in fall into the sharpest-draining, sandiest soil available; avoid organic mulch that holds moisture against the crown.

directions: A rare, mat-forming coastal dune endemic with fleshy, waxy, often curled leaves and purplish-pink flower heads that attract butterflies, growing it from responsibly sourced seed supports ex-situ conservation of a sand-mining- and invasive-species-threatened taxon while providing a genuinely low, spreading dune-garden groundcover. Full coastal sun and steady onshore air movement suit it best; inland heat without the moderating coastal influence is a poor match. Only source seed or plants from reputable native-plant nurseries given its rare-plant status and narrow range.

planting.note: Divide or sow in fall into well-drained soil with a bit more consistent moisture than most drought-adapted relatives; give it room at the front of a border or among rocks.

directions: A low, rhizomatous mat-former with tubular white-to-pink flowers, this monardella is well suited to small native-garden spaces in southern California chaparral and mountain-forest conditions, supporting bird, hummingbird, butterfly, and bee gardens as a strong multi-pollinator groundcover choice. Its rhizomatous habit lets it slowly knit together into a low tuft or mat. Moderate, regular watering through the growing season keeps the mat dense and floriferous without the crisping seen in plants pushed too dry.

planting.note: Plant responsibly sourced seed or cuttings in fall tucked among rocks or decomposed granite for sharp drainage above all else.

directions: An aromatic subshrub endemic to Mojave Desert sky-island habitats, notably Joshua Tree National Park, this monardella is valued for an unusually long bloom window from April through November depending on rainfall and for thriving in the rocky, granite-boulder conditions that challenge many other garden perennials. Its long, rainfall-dependent bloom window means a plant can flower intermittently from spring through fall if given occasional deep watering after dry spells. Because it carries a California Rare Plant Rank, source seed or nursery stock only from growers propagating responsibly collected material.
sources: National Park Service, Joshua Tree National Park
